extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, policymakers, and advocates concerned with freedom of expression, public discourse, and the cultivation of judgment
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical and practical criteria for why opinions must be freely discussed and how free discussion cultivates reliable judgment in individuals and societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrigibility of human understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of human judgement depends on the property that errors are corrigible: 'He is capable of rectifying his mistakes, by discussion and experience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion is essential because experience alone cannot be properly interpreted; the capacity to correct mistakes by exposing them to argument and experience is the source of intellectual and moral respectability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of discussion to interpret facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Very few facts can 'tell their own story' without comments to bring out their meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facts and arguments must be brought before the mind and interpreted via discussion; without commentary, facts seldom produce cognitive change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep mind open to criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: A trustworthy judgmenter 'has kept his mind open to criticism of his opinions and conduct' and listens to what can be said against him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He profits by just criticisms, exposes fallacies, and studies every mode of looking at a subject; this habit is the stable foundation for reliable judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider all varieties of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: To approach knowledge of a whole subject one must hear what can be said about it 'by persons of every variety of opinion' and study all modes of examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No wise person acquires wisdom except by collating their views with diverse opponents; refusing other perspectives undermines the claim to certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active search for objections and difficulties
rubrics_metrics.description: The best practice is 'seeking for objections and difficulties, instead of avoiding them', shutting out no light from any quarter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A position defended after such searching has a right to be trusted over positions never subjected to the same scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles protected by law must endure scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: What the wisest require to warrant relying on their judgment 'should be submitted to' by the public; even the most sacred doctrines are tested (e.g., the 'devil's advocate' in canonisation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal or public protection of beliefs that prevents questioning assumes infallibility and is unjustified; public doctrines should be open to challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: No doctrine exempt from questioning because it seems certain
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusing to allow questioning of a principle because it is thought 'so certain' amounts to assuming infallibility: 'To call any proposition certain, while there is any one who would deny its certainty if permitted, ... is to assume that we ourselves ... are the judges of certainty, and judges without hearing the other side.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If someone would deny a proposition when permitted but is not permitted, then claiming certainty is illegitimate; certainty must be tested by hearing opponents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility cannot substitute for debate about truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments for restraining discussion on the ground of an opinion's usefulness fail because 'the usefulness of an opinion is itself matter of opinion' and therefore disputable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deciding an opinion is too useful to be questioned shifts the assumption of infallibility to a different point; judgments of usefulness require the same open debate as truth-claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbidding truth-claims but allowing only usefulness-claims is incoherent
rubrics_metrics.description: It is inadequate to permit a heretic to plead only the utility or harmlessness of his belief while forbidding him to maintain its truth: 'The truth of an opinion is part of its utility.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fair discussion about usefulness cannot be complete if one side is denied the right to argue for truth; consideration of desirability must include truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persecution is not a reliable test of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that 'truth always triumphs over persecution' is false; history shows truth often suppressed by persecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (multiple historical religious movements and figures) demonstrate persecution can extinguish or delay truths for centuries; persecution is not a harmless ordeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persecution may reward benefactors with martyrdom
rubrics_metrics.description: To discover and prove new truths and be repaid by martyrdom is a perverse outcome: the propounder of a new truth should not be treated as a criminal merely because his ideas challenge the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treating introducers of new beneficial ideas with punishment is morally reprehensible and undermines social progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social stigma is an effective form of suppression
rubrics_metrics.description: Even absent severe legal penalties, social stigma and exclusion (loss of livelihood, being 'ill-thought of and ill-spoken of') effectively prevent open avowal of heterodox opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal penalties may have declined, but social penalties remain powerful and may be as damaging as law for those dependent on others' goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal rules that exclude dissenters from civic participation are unjust and self-defeating
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules barring persons (e.g., those who do not profess belief in a god) from giving evidence or serving on juries are both insulting and logically suicidal: they presume unbelievers are liars while admitting only atheists willing to lie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such exclusions are relics of persecution and cut away their own foundations; they harm both believers and nonbelievers and deny justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequence of enforced reticence: intellectual cowardice and conformism
rubrics_metrics.description: When heretics disguise opinions or avoid active diffusion, society yields 'mere conformers to commonplace, or time-servers for truth' rather than open, fearless characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The suppression of free expression narrows public discourse to small practical matters and precludes the emergence of logical, consistent intellects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free discussion cultivates the understanding and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivating intellect and judgment requires learning the grounds of one's opinions; people should 'be able to defend against at least the common objections.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching alone is insufficient except where no legitimate objections exist (e.g., mathematics); in most domains truth depends on balancing conflicting reasons, which demands exposure to challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beliefs held without understanding grounds become 'dead dogma'
rubrics_metrics.description: If an opinion is not 'fully, frequently, and fearlessly discussed' it will be held as 'a dead dogma, not a living truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even true opinions lose vitality and intellectual robustness unless continuously tested and debated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish subjects where one-sided teaching suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: In subjects like mathematics where 'there is nothing at all to be said on the wrong side,' teaching that omits controversy may suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In most human concerns (morals, religion, politics) there are competing explanations; thus those topics require adversarial examination to understand grounds for belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the adversary's case thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Cicero's practice, one ought to study the adversary's case 'with as great, if not with still greater, intensity than even his own.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitating such study is essential to arrive at truth; much of argument consists in dispelling appearances that favor competing opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing discussion assumes infallibility even when sincerely held
rubrics_metrics.description: Denying a hearing to those one sincerely thinks immoral or impious is still 'assuming infallibility' and is particularly dangerous because it often leads to historical miscarriages of justice (e.g., Socrates, early Christians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when convictions are strongest, enforcing them by preventing contrary argument is both objectionable and perilous for society.

rubrics_metrics.name: The public benefit from keeping intellectual 'lists' open
rubrics_metrics.description: Beliefs have 'no safeguard to rest on, but a standing invitation to the whole world to prove them unfounded'—keeping the lists open gives the best chance for truth to be found or defended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open challenge is the sole practical way for fallible beings to approach certainty; even if challenges fail, keeping debate open is the best method available.
